claim: Mcm1 cis-regulatory sites evolved independently at the ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) in several yeast lineages.
source: Previously, genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation and bioinformatics experiments revealed that Mcm1 cis-regulatory sites evolved independently at the ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) in several yeast lineages (Tuch et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tuch et al., 2008a

claim: Mcm1 sites were found highly enriched at the RPGs in six different monophyletic groups including the clades represented by Kluyveromyces lactis, Candida glabrata, and Yarrowia lipolytica, as well as the individual species Kazachstania naganishii, Pachysolen tannophilus, and Arthrobotrys oligospora.
source: Mcm1 sites were found highly enriched (-log10(P) > 6) at the RPGs in six different monophyletic groups including the clades represented by Kluyveromyces lactis, Candida glabrata, and Yarrowia lipolytica, as well as the individual species Kazachstania naganishii, Pachysolen tannophilus, and Arthrobotrys oligospora.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of 162 sequenced fungal genomes as described in the manuscript

claim: Mcm1 sites were found moderately enriched in the RPGs in seven additional lineages.
source: Mcm1 sites were found moderately enriched (6 > -log10(P) > 3) in the RPGs in seven additional lineages.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of 162 sequenced fungal genomes

claim: The number of gains of Mcm1 sites at RPGs was estimated to be 13.4 under the equal rates model and 12.0 under the different rates model.
source: Under both models, the number of gains was substantial: an average of 13.4 and 12.0 for the equal and different rates models, respectively (95% highest posterior density interval of 12 – 14 and 7 – 17 gains, respectively).
evidence: Supported by stochastic character mapping analysis using two evolutionary models

claim: The number of losses of Mcm1 sites differed between models, with an average of 3.0 losses for the equal rates model and 17.0 for the different rates model.
source: The number of losses differed between the models resulting in an average of 3.0 losses for the equal rates model and 17.0 for the different rates model.
evidence: Supported by stochastic character mapping analysis

claim: Scrambling the Mcm1 cis-regulatory sites in Kl. lactis RPL37 and RPS18 reporters reduced expression of the reporter.
source: In both cases, the scrambled site reduced expression of the reporter (RPS18 p=0.017; RPL37 p=0.027; Welch's t-test) but left the cell-to-cell variability unchanged (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays in Kl. lactis

claim: Mcm1 plays a non-redundant role in activating ribosomal protein genes in Kl. lactis under conditions that require high expression of the translational machinery.
source: Given that there are many known regulators of ribosomal protein transcription, this demonstrates that Mcm1 plays a non-redundant role in activating these genes in Kl. lactis under conditions that require high expression of the translational machinery.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observation that scrambling Mcm1 sites reduces expression

claim: Yeast ribosomes are composed of four ribosomal RNAs and 78 ribosomal proteins, assembled in equal stoichiometry.
source: Yeast ribosomes are composed of four ribosomal RNAs and 78 ribosomal proteins, assembled in equal stoichiometry (Woolford and Baserga, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolford and Baserga, 2013

claim: In rapidly growing cells, ribosomal protein transcripts are among the most highly expressed, and have short half-lives.
source: In rapidly growing cells, ribosomal protein transcripts are among the most highly expressed, and have short half-lives, leading to the estimation that approximately 50% of all RNA polymerase II initiation events occur at ribosomal proteins (Warner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner, 1999

claim: Approximately 50% of all RNA polymerase II initiation events occur at ribosomal proteins in rapidly growing yeast cells.
source: In rapidly growing cells, ribosomal protein transcripts are among the most highly expressed, and have short half-lives, leading to the estimation that approximately 50% of all RNA polymerase II initiation events occur at ribosomal proteins (Warner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner, 1999

claim: The expression of ribosomal protein genes is under strong selection as it plays a major role in energy expenditure in the cell.
source: These observations suggest that the expression of these genes is under strong selection as it plays a major role in energy expenditure in the cell.
evidence: Inferred from the high expression levels and energy costs of ribosomal protein transcription

claim: In both Kl. lactis × Kl. marxianus and Kl. lactis × Kl. wickerhamii hybrids, the ribosomal protein genes showed evidence for cis-regulatory evolution.
source: In both hybrids, the RPGs showed evidence for cis-regulatory evolution (hypergeometric test, p=2.36e-3 for Kl. lactis × Kl. marxianus hybrid; p=1.52e-6 for Kl. lactis × Kl. wickerhamii hybrid).
evidence: Supported by allele-specific expression data from interspecies hybrids

claim: In both hybrids, the ribosomal protein genes were expressed, on average, lower in the Kl. lactis alleles than in alleles of either of the other species.
source: However, in both hybrids, the ribosomal protein genes were expressed, on average, lower in the Kl. lactis alleles than in alleles of either of the other species.
evidence: Supported by allele-specific expression data from interspecies hybrids

claim: The observation that Kl. lactis RPG alleles are expressed lower than other species rules out the hypothesis that the gain of Mcm1 sites was simply due to directional selection to increase expression of the ribosomal proteins as a whole.
source: This observation rules out the hypothesis that the gain of Mcm1 sites over this timescale was simply due to directional selection to increase expression of the ribosomal proteins as a whole (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the allele-specific expression data showing lower expression in Kl. lactis

claim: Ongoing evolution of Mcm1 sites in the Kluyveromyces clade compensates for other cis-regulatory changes that reduce RPG transcript levels.
source: Instead, it favors the second hypothesis: ongoing evolution of Mcm1 sites in the Kluyveromyces clade compensates (perhaps incompletely) for other cis-regulatory changes that reduce RPG transcript levels.
evidence: Inferred from the allele-specific expression data and the observation of reduced binding sites for other regulators

claim: The binding sites for other regulators (including Fhl1 and Rrn7) show a reduction in the Kluyveromyces clade.
source: A compensatory model is consistent with the observation that the binding sites for other regulators (including Fhl1 and Rrn7) show a reduction in the Kluyveromyces clade (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site distributions

claim: In all published yeast interspecies hybrid experiments from the Saccharomyces clade, the ribosomal proteins were among the sets of genes with reported directional cis-regulatory evolution.
source: Surprisingly, in all cases, the ribosomal proteins were among the sets of genes with reported directional cis-regulatory evolution (Bullard et al., 2010; Clowers et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple published studies

claim: RPG expression may frequently experience different evolutionary forces between closely related yeast species.
source: These observations demonstrate that RPG expression may frequently experience different evolutionary forces between closely related yeast species, and they are consistent with the high rate of gains and losses of cis-regulatory sequences that control RPG transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of directional cis-regulatory evolution in multiple interspecies hybrids

claim: In Kl. lactis, the Mcm1 sites were gained a fixed distance away from the binding site for Rap1.
source: We previously noted that, in Kl. lactis, the Mcm1 sites were gained a fixed distance away from the binding site for another transcription regulator, Rap1, whose sites at the RPGs were ancestral to Kl. lactis and S. cerevisiae (Tuch et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tuch et al., 2008a

claim: The spacing between Mcm1 and Rap1 sites was particularly precise with peaks at 54, 65, and 74 basepairs apart, favoring a configuration with the two proteins on the same side of the DNA helix.
source: By pooling data from additional species with Rap1-Mcm1 sites, we discovered that the spacing between Mcm1 and Rap1 sites was particularly precise with peaks at 54, 65, and 74 basepairs apart, favoring a configuration with the two proteins on the same side of the DNA helix (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site spacing across multiple species

claim: The transcriptional output of RPS17 reporter constructs showed sensitivity to spacing between the Rap1 and Mcm1 sites.
source: The transcriptional output of this second series of constructs showed sensitivity to spacing between the sites (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays with varying spacing

claim: KlMcm1 and KlRap1 activated transcription cooperatively in Kl. lactis: their combined expression was approximately four times the sum of their individual contributions.
source: Deletion of the Mcm1 and Rap1 binding sites individually and in combination showed that the proteins KlMcm1 and KlRap1 activated transcription cooperatively in Kl. lactis: their combined expression was approximately four times the sum of their individual contributions (Figure 3F; p=5.5e-4, one sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays with site deletions

claim: ScRap1 and ScMcm1 activated expression of the Kl. lactis Rap1-Mcm1 reporter cooperatively in S. cerevisiae.
source: We found that ScRap1 and ScMcm1 activated expression of the reporter cooperatively (p=3.9e-3, one sample t-test), thereby demonstrating that these proteins have the capacity to work together even in a species where their binding sites did not evolve close proximity (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays in S. cerevisiae

claim: The ability of Rap1 and Mcm1 to activate transcription cooperatively was ancestral, existing even in species that did not take advantage of it in regulating the RPGs.
source: This result rejects the derived cooperativity model and strongly suggests that the ability of Rap1 and Mcm1 to activate transcription cooperatively was ancestral, existing even in species that did not take advantage of it in regulating the RPGs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that S. cerevisiae Rap1 and Mcm1 cooperate despite lacking Mcm1 sites at RPGs

claim: Purified full-length S. cerevisiae and Kl. lactis Rap1 and Mcm1 proteins bound to the RPG promoter DNA independently and did not appear to increase the other's affinity.
source: In all cases, each protein bound to the RPG promoter DNA independently and did not appear to increase the other's affinity, indicating that Rap1 and Mcm1 do not, on their own, bind DNA cooperatively (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gel-mobility shift assay data

claim: Rap1 and Mcm1 do not bind DNA cooperatively on their own.
source: In all cases, each protein bound to the RPG promoter DNA independently and did not appear to increase the other's affinity, indicating that Rap1 and Mcm1 do not, on their own, bind DNA cooperatively (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gel-mobility shift assay data

claim: The direct interaction of Rap1 with TFIID is required for RPG transcription in S. cerevisiae.
source: TFIID is a general transcription factor whose direct interaction with Rap1 is required for RPG transcription in S. cerevisiae (Garbett et al., 2007; Layer et al., 2010; Mencía et al., 2002; Papai et al., 2010; Reja et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: TFIID activates transcription through contacts with RNA Polymerase II, and its binding to the promoter is a rate-limiting step in the activation of TFIID-dependent genes.
source: Furthermore, TFIID activates transcription through contacts with RNA Polymerase II, and its binding to the promoter is a rate-limiting step in the activation of TFIID-dependent genes (Wu and Chiang, 2001), such as the RPGs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu and Chiang, 2001

claim: The interaction between the 'activation domain' of Rap1 and the Taf5 subunit of TFIID is important, as mutations that compromise this interaction strongly reduce ribosomal protein gene transcription.
source: Of particular importance is the interaction between the 'activation domain' of Rap1 and the Taf5 subunit of TFIID, as mutations that compromise this interaction strongly reduce ribosomal protein gene transcription (Johnson and Weil, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson and Weil, 2017

claim: Mcm1 binds directly to the Taf4 subunit of TFIID.
source: We found that Mcm1 binds directly to the Taf4 subunit (Figure 4B,C); using deletions of Taf4, we further mapped the interaction to the N-terminal region of Taf4 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by Far-Western protein-protein binding assay data

claim: The Mcm1 binding domain on Taf4 is located in the N-terminal region of Taf4.
source: We found that Mcm1 binds directly to the Taf4 subunit (Figure 4B,C); using deletions of Taf4, we further mapped the interaction to the N-terminal region of Taf4 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by Far-Western protein-protein binding assay data with Taf4 deletions

claim: Rap1 binds to Taf4 in the C-terminus of this subunit, distinct from the Mcm1 interaction site.
source: Although Rap1 also binds to Taf4 (in addition to Taf5 and Taf12), its target is in the C-terminus of this subunit, distinct from the Mcm1 interaction site.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previous studies and the current mapping of Mcm1 binding domain

claim: The finding that Rap1 and Mcm1 both interact with distinct domains of TFIID provides a simple explanation for their ability to activate transcription cooperatively.
source: The finding that Rap1 and Mcm1 both interact with distinct domains of a common component of the transcription machinery, one whose assembly at the promoter is rate limiting, provides a simple explanation for their ability to activate transcription cooperatively.
evidence: Inferred from the biochemical data showing distinct binding sites on TFIID

claim: Rap1AS shows cooperative transcriptional activation with Mcm1.
source: As shown in Figure 5A–C, Rap1AS shows cooperative transcriptional activation with Mcm1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from growth assays with HIS3 reporter

claim: Mutations in the activation domain of Rap1AS (Rap1AS7Ala) strongly reduced growth on media containing 3-aminotriazole, indicating that efficient expression requires an intact Rap1 activation domain.
source: When introduced in the presence of the Rap1-Mcm1 HIS3 reporter, these mutations strongly reduced growth on media containing 3-aminotriazole (3-AT), a competitive inhibitor of the HIS3 gene product (Brennan and Struhl, 1980), indicating that efficient expression requires an intact Rap1 activation domain (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from growth assays with mutant Rap1

claim: The cooperative transcriptional activation by Rap1 and Mcm1 at the RPGs is due to both proteins interacting with TFIID.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that the cooperative transcriptional activation by Rap1 and Mcm1 at the RPGs in these clades is due to both proteins interacting with TFIID, a component of the general transcriptional machinery.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of biochemical and genetic experiments

claim: Ka. naganishii had 33 genes with Rap1-Mcm1 sites at similar spacing and orientation to that observed in the RPGs.
source: Most species analyzed had only a few such genes of questionable significance, but Ka. naganishii had 33, showing that Rap1 and Mcm1 sites can evolve at genes other than the RPGs.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of genome-wide promoters

claim: Most of the sub-optimal Mcm1 sites displayed near wild-type levels of expression in the presence—but not in the absence—of neighboring Rap1 sites.
source: Consistent with the prediction, most of the sub-optimal Mcm1 sites displayed near wild-type levels of expression in the presence—but not in the absence—of neighboring Rap1 sites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays with weak Mcm1 sites

claim: In some clades, Mcm1 sites were gained varying distances away from the pre-existing sites of other regulators (Tbf1, Rrn7, and Fhl1).
source: This analysis revealed that, in some of these clades, Mcm1 sites were gained varying distances away from the pre-existing sites of other regulators (Tbf1, Rrn7, and Fhl1), suggesting that the evolutionary mechanism we identified with Rap1 and Mcm1 might be a generalizable to other instances of cis-regulatory evolution (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site locations relative to Mcm1

claim: Tbf1, Rrn7, and Fhl1 are reported to interact (directly or indirectly) with TFIID.
source: Consistent with this idea, all three of these regulators are reported to interact (directly or indirectly) with TFIID (Gavin et al., 2002; Knutson et al., 2014; Mallick and Whiteway, 2013; Zhong and Melcher, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The relationship between Rap1 and Mcm1 by virtue of their interaction with different surfaces of TFIID is ancient.
source: This relationship between Rap1 and Mcm1 is ancient, and in the next section, we discuss how this property can predispose transcription networks to evolve repeatedly along the same trajectory.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cooperativity exists in species without Mcm1 sites at RPGs

claim: In three lineages, Mcm1 binding sites were gained a fixed distance from the sites for Rap1.
source: In three of these lineages, Mcm1 binding sites were gained a fixed distance from the sites for another transcription regulator, Rap1, and we show that these newly acquired Mcm1 sites are required for full activation of the RPGs.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site spacing and experimental validation

claim: The newly acquired Mcm1 sites are required for full activation of the RPGs.
source: In three of these lineages, Mcm1 binding sites were gained a fixed distance from the sites for another transcription regulator, Rap1, and we show that these newly acquired Mcm1 sites are required for full activation of the RPGs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from reporter assays showing reduced expression when Mcm1 sites are scrambled

claim: Mcm1 and Rap1 cooperatively activate ribosomal protein genes.
source: We also show that Mcm1 and Rap1 cooperatively activate these genes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from reporter assays with site deletions

claim: The direct interaction of both Rap1 and Mcm1 with TFIID provides a plausible mechanism for cooperative transcription activation.
source: The direct interaction of both of these regulators with a common target, the general transcription factor TFIID, provides a plausible mechanism for this cooperative transcription activation.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical data showing both proteins bind TFIID

claim: The ability of Rap1 and Mcm1 to work together was ancestral to the more recent gains of Mcm1 sites adjacent to Rap1 sites at the RPGs.
source: It also explains why the ability of Rap1 and Mcm1 to work together was ancestral to the more recent gains of Mcm1 sites adjacent to Rap1 sites at the RPGs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that S. cerevisiae proteins cooperate despite lacking Mcm1 sites at RPGs

claim: The yeast species with Mcm1 sites at the RPGs are from diverse ecological niches and utilize different nutrient sources.
source: However, the yeast species with Mcm1 sites at the RPGs are from diverse ecological niches (e.g. plant leaves, mangrove sediment, the human body, soil) and utilize different nutrient sources (e.g. lactate, xylose, feline skin, nematode predation), defying a specific environmental adaptation explanation.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the ecological characteristics of the species analyzed

claim: A species in which the Mcm1 sites were gained at the RPGs does not express these genes at higher levels than related species that evolved fewer Mcm1 sites.
source: Consistent with this view is our observation, based on analyzing interspecies hybrids, that a species in which the Mcm1 sites were gained at the RPGs does not express these genes at higher levels than related species that evolved fewer Mcm1 sites.
evidence: Supported by allele-specific expression data from interspecies hybrids

claim: In the Kluyveromyces-Saccharomyces ancestor (before the parallel gains of Mcm1 sites) Rap1 bound to the ribosomal protein genes and activated transcription through interactions with TFIID.
source: Specifically, we propose that, in the Kluyveromyces-Saccharomyces ancestor (before the parallel gains of Mcm1 sites) Rap1 bound to the ribosomal protein genes and activated transcription through interactions with TFIID, as it does in extant species.
evidence: Inferred from observations in extant species and evolutionary analysis

claim: In the ancestor, Mcm1 activated non-ribosomal genes by interaction with a second site on TFIID.
source: We further propose that, in the ancestor, Mcm1 activated non-ribosomal genes by interaction with a second site on TFIID, as it does in the extant species S. cerevisiae.
evidence: Inferred from observations in extant species

claim: Any suboptimal Mcm1 site that arose by chance point mutation at a specified distance from a Rap1 site would immediately be functional because even a weak Mcm1 DNA interaction would be stabilized by Mcm1's intrinsic ability to directly bind TFIID.
source: Any suboptimal Mcm1 site that arose by chance point mutation at a specified distance from a Rap1 site would immediately be functional (Figure 7) because, as we show, even a weak Mcm1 DNA interaction would be stabilized by Mcm1's intrinsic ability to directly bind TFIID (see Figure 4C and 6A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing weak Mcm1 sites are functional with Rap1

claim: The appearance of Mcm1 sites likely occurred concomitantly with the gradual losses of other cis-regulatory sites in the RPGs.
source: The appearance of Mcm1 sites likely occurred concomitantly with the gradual losses of other cis-regulatory sites in the RPGs; in other words, the Mcm1 cis-regulatory sites would fall under selection as other cis-regulatory sites deteriorated by mutation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced binding sites for other regulators

claim: The free energy gained from the intrinsic interaction between Mcm1 and TFIID would favor formation of new Mcm1 sites at the expense of pre-existing cis-regulatory sequences.
source: In essence, we propose that the free energy gained from the intrinsic interaction between Mcm1 and TFIID would favor formation of new Mcm1 sites at the expense of pre-existing cis-regulatory sequences, particularly since the latter provide a larger target for inactivating mutations.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on thermodynamic principles and the experimental observations

claim: This model accounts for why Mcm1 sites (and not those of other transcription regulators) were repeatedly gained at the RPGs and why the distance between Rap1 and Mcm1 sites is constrained.
source: This model accounts for why Mcm1 sites (and not those of other transcription regulators) were repeatedly gained at the RPGs and why the distance between Rap1 and Mcm1 sites is constrained in those species in which the gains occurred.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple lines of evidence

claim: Cooperative transcriptional activation by Mcm1 and Rap1 requires the activation domain of Rap1, which is known to interact with TFIID.
source: (3) cooperative transcriptional activation by Mcm1 and Rap1 requires the activation domain of Rap1, which is known to interact with TFIID;
evidence: Supported by experimental data with Rap1 activation domain mutants

claim: The spacing between Rap1 and Mcm1 sites in the ribosomal protein genes places the proteins on the same side of the helix but at least 50 bp apart, consistent with a physical interaction with a large complex.
source: (4) the spacing between Rap1 and Mcm1 sites in the ribosomal protein genes places the proteins on the same side of the helix but at least 50 bp apart, consistent with a physical interaction with a large complex;
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site spacing

claim: Engineered suboptimal Mcm1 sites are functional as long as they are adjacent to Rap1 sites.
source: (5) engineered suboptimal Mcm1 sites are functional as long as they are adjacent to Rap1 sites;
evidence: Supported by experimental data from reporter assays with weak Mcm1 sites

claim: Mcm1 and Rap1 have the intrinsic ability to cooperate (through interactions with TFIID) even in a species where Mcm1 sites were not gained at the RPGs.
source: (6) Mcm1 and Rap1 have the intrinsic ability to cooperate (through interactions with TFIID) even in a species where Mcm1 sites were not gained at the RPGs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from S. cerevisiae reporter assays

claim: This model does not require any change in Rap1 or Mcm1 during the gains of Mcm1 sites at the RPGs.
source: We note that this model does not require any change in Rap1 or Mcm1 during the gains of Mcm1 sites at the RPGs.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the ancestral cooperativity model

claim: Rap1 and Mcm1 activated many genes separately in the ancestor, thus preserving by stabilizing selection their ability to interact with TFIID.
source: Presumably, Rap1 and Mcm1 activated many genes separately in the ancestor, thus preserving by stabilizing selection their ability to interact with TFIID.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about ancestral gene regulation

claim: The transcriptional output was slightly more cooperative in Kl. lactis than in S. cerevisiae.
source: (We note that the transcriptional output was slightly more cooperative in Kl. lactis than in S. cerevisiae, leaving open the possibility that additional fine-scale evolutionary changes may have occurred in how these proteins interact.)
evidence: Inferred from comparison of reporter assay data between the two species

claim: The ability of the two regulators to work together was ancestral, part of each protein's intrinsic mechanism of transcriptional activation.
source: According to our model, the ability of the two regulators to work together was ancestral, part of each protein's intrinsic mechanism of transcriptional activation; therefore, their coupling at the RPGs would avoid such pleiotropic changes.
evidence: This is a summary of the model based on multiple lines of evidence

claim: Mcm1 cis-regulatory sequences show preferred spacing relative to known regulators of the RPGs, specifically Tbf1 and Rrn7, in clades where Rap1 does not regulate the RPGs.
source: In these cases, Mcm1 cis-regulatory sequences also show preferred spacing relative to known regulators of the RPGs, specifically Tbf1 and Rrn7, and we propose that the same type of cooperativity with TFIID can also account for these cases.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of binding site locations

claim: TFIID occupies the promoters of RPGs in human cell lines.
source: Indeed, TFIID occupies the promoters of RPGs in human cell lines as well (ENCODE Project Consortium et al., 2012), raising the possibility that TFIID is a conserved general activator of the RPGs across fungi and animals, while the specific transcription regulators that interact with TFIID simply interchange over this timescale.
evidence: Supported by citation to ENCODE Project Consortium et al., 2012

claim: TFIID may be a conserved general activator of the RPGs across fungi and animals, while the specific transcription regulators that interact with TFIID simply interchange over evolutionary timescales.
source: Indeed, TFIID occupies the promoters of RPGs in human cell lines as well (ENCODE Project Consortium et al., 2012), raising the possibility that TFIID is a conserved general activator of the RPGs across fungi and animals, while the specific transcription regulators that interact with TFIID simply interchange over this timescale.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation of TFIID at RPGs in humans

claim: Selection must have operated to preserve the Mcm1 sites as they arose in the population.
source: While our cooperative activation model provides an explanation for the parallel acquisition of Mcm1 cis-regulatory site evolution, selection must have operated to preserve the Mcm1 sites as they arose in the population.
evidence: This is a logical inference about evolutionary processes

claim: The gains of Mcm1 sites compensated for the degradation of other cis-regulatory sequences and thereby fell under selection.
source: As described earlier, we favor a model where the gains of Mcm1 sites compensated for the degradation of other cis-regulatory sequences and thereby fell under selection.
evidence: This is the authors' preferred model based on the allelic expression data

claim: The allelic expression data strongly supports a compensatory model for the Kluyveromyces clade.
source: The allelic expression data (Figure 2) strongly supports this model for one clade, represented by Kluyveromyces species.
evidence: Supported by allele-specific expression data from interspecies hybrids

claim: In other clades or over shorter timescales, the Mcm1 sites could have been gained due to selection for higher levels of RPG expression.
source: However, it is also possible that, in other clades or over shorter timescales, the Mcm1 sites could have been gained due to selection for higher levels of RPG expression.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation

claim: The widespread differences in RPG expression revealed by published interspecies hybrid experiments suggest that RPG expression may experience strong and shifting selection.
source: The widespread differences in RPG expression revealed by the published interspecies hybrid experiments suggest that RPG expression may experience strong and shifting selection, helping to account for the surprising observation that transcriptional regulators that control the RPGs vary substantially across species (Gasch et al., 2004; Lavoie et al., 2010; Mallick and Whiteway, 2013; Tanay et al., 2005; Tuch et al., 2008a; Zeevi et al., 2014; Zeevi et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from published interspecies hybrid data and cited studies

claim: Transcriptional regulators that control the RPGs vary substantially across species.
source: The widespread differences in RPG expression revealed by the published interspecies hybrid experiments suggest that RPG expression may experience strong and shifting selection, helping to account for the surprising observation that transcriptional regulators that control the RPGs vary substantially across species (Gasch et al., 2004; Lavoie et al., 2010; Mallick and Whiteway, 2013; Tanay et al., 2005; Tuch et al., 2008a; Zeevi et al., 2014; Zeevi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The intrinsic cooperativity model is sufficient to explain the gain of Mcm1 sites whether or not any change in selection occurs.
source: We note that the intrinsic cooperativity model is sufficient to explain the gain of Mcm1 sites whether or not any change in selection occurs: if functional Mcm1 sites are relatively easy to form (because of intrinsic cooperativity) they will be favored over gains of other cis-regulatory sequences by mutational processes alone.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model's explanatory power

claim: If functional Mcm1 sites are relatively easy to form (because of intrinsic cooperativity) they will be favored over gains of other cis-regulatory sequences by mutational processes alone.
source: We note that the intrinsic cooperativity model is sufficient to explain the gain of Mcm1 sites whether or not any change in selection occurs: if functional Mcm1 sites are relatively easy to form (because of intrinsic cooperativity) they will be favored over gains of other cis-regulatory sequences by mutational processes alone.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about mutational bias

claim: Mutations creating Mcm1 sites and weakening other sites could occur sequentially in either order or simultaneously (on the same haplotype), depending on the expression requirements of the RPG at that point in its evolutionary history.
source: Mutations creating Mcm1 sites and weakening other sites could occur sequentially in either order or simultaneously (on the same haplotype), depending on the expression requirements of the RPG at that point in its evolutionary history.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the order of mutational events

claim: Most or all of the selection scenarios outlined have likely occurred in at least one RPG at some point during the multiple and ongoing gains of Mcm1 sites over millions of years of fungal evolution.
source: We feel that it is likely that most or all of the selection scenarios outlined above have occurred in at least one RPG at some point during the multiple and ongoing gains of Mcm1 sites over millions of years of fungal evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the diversity of evolutionary scenarios

claim: Intrinsic cooperativity biases the RPGs as a whole toward gaining Mcm1 sites.
source: While the precise circumstances of each Mcm1 site gain are unknown, intrinsic cooperativity biases the RPGs as a whole toward gaining these sites.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating the model and observations

claim: The parallel gains of Mcm1 sites at the ribosomal genes do not require an extraordinary mechanism beyond individual point mutations in the cis-regulatory region of each gene.
source: Although, on the surface, the parallel gains of Mcm1 sites at the ribosomal genes would seem to require a special evolutionary explanation, our model does not require an extraordinary mechanism beyond individual point mutations in the cis-regulatory region of each gene.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's implications

claim: The ancestral ability of Rap1 and Mcm1 to activate transcription simplifies the path to gaining Mcm1 sites by producing a phenotypic output from even non-optimal sites.
source: However, the ancestral ability of the two key regulators to activate transcription simplifies the path to gaining these sites by producing a phenotypic output from even non-optimal sites.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating experimental observations

claim: Mcm1 can significantly activate transcription at the ribosomal proteins more easily than it would elsewhere in the genome because of its intrinsic ability to cooperate with Rap1.
source: Mcm1, because of its intrinsic ability to cooperate with Rap1, can significantly activate transcription at the ribosomal proteins more easily than it would elsewhere in the genome; likewise, Mcm1 (or another regulator that interacted with TFIID) would be preferred at the RPGs over regulators that did not share this common direct protein interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the intrinsic cooperativity model

claim: Mcm1 (or another regulator that interacted with TFIID) would be preferred at the RPGs over regulators that did not share this common direct protein interaction.
source: Mcm1, because of its intrinsic ability to cooperate with Rap1, can significantly activate transcription at the ribosomal proteins more easily than it would elsewhere in the genome; likewise, Mcm1 (or another regulator that interacted with TFIID) would be preferred at the RPGs over regulators that did not share this common direct protein interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the intrinsic cooperativity model

claim: The intrinsic cooperativity of Rap1 and Mcm1 'channels' random mutations into functional Mcm1 cis-regulatory sequences, accounting for the observed parallel evolution.

claim: Gene activation through intrinsic cooperativity may be a general mechanism to explain the rapid and ubiquitous rewiring of transcription networks.
